summary: This informational RFC reports on an IAB workshop, Interconnecting Smart Objects with the Internet, held in Prague on 25 March 2011. It gathered feedback on deploying IETF protocols in constrained environments and lists conclusions.

eli5.summary: A meeting of experts about connecting tiny smart gadgets to the internet. This is the notes of what they said.

questions: interconnecting smart objects with the internet
what are the challenges of internet of things
how do constrained devices use protocols
what is the smart object workshop
subtitle: Report from a 2011 workshop on connecting tiny, battery-powered devices to the internet.

tldr.problem: Billions of embedded devices with limited power, memory, and bandwidth now need internet connectivity. Existing protocols designed for powerful computers are often too heavy for these constrained devices, and key challenges like energy efficiency, security, and routing remain unsolved.
tldr.mechanism: This workshop brought together IETF researchers and engineers to share experiences deploying internet protocols on constrained devices, identify unsolved problems, and recommend new work. It covered architectural questions, energy concerns, security, and routing for low-power and lossy networks.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified multiple areas needing new standards, including a new routing protocol (RPL) for lossy networks, lightweight crypto primitives, energy-aware protocol design, and frameworks for home and building networks.

facts.label: Main outcome
facts.value: RPL routing protocol for low-power networks

today: RFC 6574 remains the definitive workshop report. The outcomes it recommended have largely come to pass: RPL was standardized as RFC 6550, ROLL and LWIG working groups have produced standards, and HOMENET and CFRG continue to address smart object needs. The Internet of Things has grown far larger than predicted in 2011, and energy efficiency remains a critical design constraint.

sections.title: Connecting Smart Objects to the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet once connected powerful computers operated by humans. Today, billions of embedded devices—sensors in buildings, lights, thermostats, meters, and industrial equipment—now connect to the internet. These devices must work with far fewer resources: they run on batteries that last months or years, have kilobytes of memory instead of gigabytes, and use low-power radios with limited bandwidth. The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to this trend of bringing embedded devices into the connected world.

Many of these devices can run standard internet protocols like IPv6, UDP, and HTTP, but they must be simplified or redesigned to fit the constraints. This workshop, held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in Prague on March 25, 2011, gathered over 70 position papers from researchers and developers implementing such systems. The goal was to surface common problems, identify where standards were needed, and suggest new work for the IETF and broader research community.
sections.eli5: Tiny computers that run on batteries now talk to the internet, but they cannot use the same software as your laptop. Experts met to figure out what to change.

sections.title: Constraints and Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
Constrained devices face multiple overlapping limits. Energy constraints mean batteries must last months; every transmission and radio wake-up drains power, so devices sleep 99% or more of the time. Memory constraints limit code size—some devices have only 2 KB of RAM and 32 KB of flash. Bandwidth constraints come from low-power radios like IEEE 802.15.4, which offer only 20 to 900 kilobits per second with high packet loss. CPU constraints limit how much computation can happen quickly.

These constraints create difficult trade-offs. A secure handshake might be computationally expensive but required for safety. A verbose protocol might be clearer but wastes bandwidth. Sleeping to save power delays responses. When a device wakes from sleep, it may have lost its network address, forcing a costly re-registration. The workshop participants emphasized that Moore's Law delivers less benefit in embedded systems than in PCs: gains go into lower cost and power, not faster processors.
sections.eli5: These devices have tiny batteries, tiny memories, and slow radios. Making them work means choosing between safety, speed, and power use.

sections.title: Architectural Challenges
sections.content:
Workshop participants debated fundamental architectural questions. One question was whether smart objects should sit on the same network as regular internet traffic, or in separate "islands." A smart grid, for example, might want isolation from guest WiFi. But separation also means losing the interoperability benefits the internet provides. The workshop concluded that both approaches should be possible without forcing loss of interoperability.

Another debate concerned protocol stacks. Different application domains—building automation, healthcare, smart grids—might need different combinations of protocols. Standardizing a unique stack for each domain is expensive; finding a common foundation for all is hard. A third question was at which protocol layer to put functionality. The internet's end-to-end principle says logic should be in endpoints, not networks. But some designers want to put application-layer features like name-based routing into lower layers for performance. The workshop could not reach agreement on these architectural questions.
sections.eli5: Should smart objects be on the main internet or separate networks? Should each kind of device use different protocols, or should they share a common foundation? Nobody fully agreed.

sections.title: Energy and Sleeping Devices
sections.content:
Most protocols assume devices are always on, waiting for incoming messages. Smart objects cannot afford this. They sleep periodically, wake only to check for events, and immediately go back to sleep. This saves energy but breaks many protocol assumptions. A device waking from sleep may find its address is no longer unique, requiring a new address to be obtained—a costly process. Protocols need to be redesigned to work with devices that are offline most of the time.

The workshop identified four design principles for energy-conscious systems: rethink the always-on assumption by letting devices explicitly advertise sleep cycles; reduce network attachment costs by minimizing the overhead of rejoining after sleep; use simple, non-verbose protocols that require fewer round-trips and shorter messages; and consider system-wide efficiency rather than optimizing individual devices in isolation.
sections.eli5: Devices that sleep most of the time cannot follow protocols that expect them to always be listening. Protocols need to be lighter and faster.

sections.title: Security, Cryptography, and Key Management
sections.content:
Security cannot be an afterthought, but constrained devices have limited CPU, memory, and power. Cryptographic operations are expensive, and choosing lightweight alternatives is tricky. The workshop recommended surveying existing authentication mechanisms for suitability in constrained environments, researching lightweight cryptographic primitives, and investigating credential management and deployment. Offloading some security computation to more powerful devices was proposed as an option.

A deeper challenge is key management. How do billions of devices get certificates or keys installed securely without user intervention? Complex solutions require user understanding they may not have. The workshop highlighted that while choosing specialized cryptographic algorithms might offer 20% CPU savings, such savings alone are unlikely to drive adoption. IPR barriers, deployment latency, and integration challenges matter as much as performance.
sections.eli5: Keeping data secret on tiny computers is hard because the math is slow and the devices have little memory. It's also hard to install secrets safely without humans having to configure each device.

sections.title: Outcomes and Next Steps
sections.content:
The workshop identified multiple areas for new standardization work. These included a new routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks (leading to RPL, the IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks), energy-aware protocol design guidelines, lightweight cryptographic research, and extensions to discovery protocols. It also identified the need for architectural guidance from the IAB on how to combine existing internet protocols in smart object environments.

Follow-up working groups and research groups were proposed or subsequently created, including ROLL for routing, LWIG for lightweight implementation guidance, HOMENET for home networking, and CFRG for cryptographic research. The workshop succeeded in giving the IETF community a shared understanding of smart object constraints and the engineering challenges they pose.
sections.eli5: The workshop said the IETF should make a new routing protocol for slow networks, design protocols that use less power, find simpler ways to do security, and help people understand how to wire tiny devices together.
